source.title: Gated Attention Blocks: Preliminary Progress toward Removing Attention Head Superposition

record.file_problem: The supplied text includes the article and appendices, but not the contents of the referenced figures.
record.tranche_reason: The study develops and evaluates a gated-attention method to resolve attention-head superposition in toy skip-trigram models. It does not test the listed versions of feature superposition, polysemanticity, SAE features, or feature dimensionality.
record.gate_note: Reported results concern attention-head superposition in OV-incoherent skip-trigram toys, a related but distinct construct from the listed claim versions. Figure contents are unavailable in the supplied text; rows below rely on explicit textual descriptions. Cited findings from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study borrows the superposition concept for attention heads in toy skip-trigram models and mainly reports how well its own gated-attention method removes it. It does not measure feature directions, sparsity transitions, neuron polysemanticity, SAE features or feature dimensionality, so no listed version is tested. The observation that one representation is spread across 4 heads (R1) is a related but different construct: cross-head interference, not features in an activation space.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that gated attention blocks resolve OV-incoherent attention-head superposition in toy single-layer models, mapping each representation to one head. They leave LLM settings, other forms of head superposition, hyperparameter sweeps and controls to future work.
record.recipe_differences: This is not a reproduction of Toy Models of Superposition. It studies attention-head interference on OV-incoherent skip-trigram toy tasks and trains an expanded gated-attention architecture with an L0.6 sparsity penalty.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that a too-high L0.6 coefficient caused no representations to be learned, while a too-low coefficient did not remove attention-head superposition; they did not conduct a systematic hyperparameter sweep.

fits_no_version.finding: In an SGD-trained 1-layer 4-head attention-only toy model with 5 OV-incoherent skip trigrams, 4 representations sat in single heads and 1 was spread across all 4 heads. A sparsity-penalised gated block with 8 heads then assigned each representation to a single head; similar results are reported for two other toy configurations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attention blocks can encode more skip-trigram behaviours than heads through cross-head interference (attention-head superposition), and a sparsity-gated expanded block can separate these behaviours into individual heads in toy settings.

record.problems: The authors say they did not extensively compare controls such as an expanded traditional attention block or a gated block without the sparsity penalty. They report no systematic hyperparameter sweep or numerical reconstruction-loss results, and note that equivalent internal behavior between original and gated blocks was not extensively studied. Experiments use toy, single-layer attention-only models and cover only OV-incoherent skip-trigram superposition; the authors leave other forms and LLM settings untested.
record.rows_left_out: No figure-only values were extracted because the referenced figures are not present in the supplied text. The article mentions additional manually specified cases in the codebase but does not provide separate textual outcome details for them.

untested.parts: No test of sparse features as nearly orthogonal directions, a sparsity-dependent transition, or geometry.
No test of neuron polysemanticity arising from capacity competition or feature importance.
No test of polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure.
No LLM measurements and no SAE feature recovery.
No test of whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical.

record.verdict_notes: Figures are unavailable, so all rows rest on textual statements. The study also notes that in the SGD-trained models the interference mechanism did not strictly match the hand-specified OV-incoherent mechanism, and the authors did not investigate it further.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test sparse features represented as nearly orthogonal directions, a sparsity-dependent transition, or regular feature geometry.
It studies attention-head representations, not whether neuron polysemanticity results from feature competition for capacity or whether feature importance determines sharing.
It does not investigate polysemantic neurons arising through other causes.
The experiments are toy models, not LLM feature-distribution or SAE-recovery measurements.
The study does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical.
It does not test whether the underlying features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional.
